description: As a Unity game developer and visual designer, I specialize in 3D modeling and creating immersive interactive experiences for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. I’m looking for team members with game development experience, strong coding fundamentals, 3D design skills, and powerful storytelling ability to build a compelling project together.
summary:
Celestial Colonies is a 2.5D colony simulation for ages 7–12, built in Unity 6 with C#. Players run an outpost on the Moon or Mars, balancing oxygen, water, power, food and radiation. Every system is input-gated — oxygen generators need ice, power plants need fuel, shields need power. No input, no output. Colonists are autonomous, evaluating priorities each cycle: crisis, repair, rest, mining. Solar events use real NASA DONKI data, including the X8.7 flare of May 2024.

Benefits: makes real engineering trade-offs tangible through play rather than explanation. Replayable, low barrier to entry, plain-language labels.

Impact: space STEM usually oversimplifies trade-offs. Here every choice costs something, so a child leaves understanding a genuine constraint of deep-space survival.

Tools: Unity 6 URP, C#, Visual Studio, NASA DONKI API, Stitch AI, Descript, ElevenLabs.

Creative: a cascade model wiring systems into a dependency graph; real flare data driving gameplay; emergent priority-driven AI; terrain-following roads; per-instance interiors.

Considered: readability for ages 7–12, no free choices, radiation and comms delay as mechanics, and honest scope over feature-stuffing.
details:
Celestial Colonies is a 2.5D colony management simulation built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge by Team Red Rocket, comprising Abhishek Das as team lead and Orchisman Som as team member. The project targets children aged seven to twelve, with flexibility to engage older siblings, parents and classroom settings.

What it does and how it works. The player establishes and sustains an off-world outpost on either the Moon at Mare Tranquillitatis or Mars at Valles Marineris. Five interdependent life-support systems are simulated in parallel: oxygen, water, power, food and radiation. Construction is grid-based, with placement validated against terrain slope, mineral deposits, existing structures, road coverage and painted terrain detail. Buildings can be rotated, demolished and refunded. Roads are painted by dragging across terrain and grant a fifty percent movement speed boost to colonists, with the navigation system calculating whether a detour onto the road actually saves time before committing to it. Roads and buildings block each other, making colony layout a genuine design decision.

Every system is input-gated. Oxygen generators consume ice to produce oxygen and water. Power plants consume fuel to produce power. Hydroponics consume power to produce food. Radiation shields consume power to absorb solar radiation during events. No input means no output, and the colony begins to drain. Population scaling means every spawned colonist raises demand across all four life-support systems, so growth is never free.

Colonists are autonomous rather than scripted. Each evaluates work in a strict priority order every cycle: crisis resolution first, then repair, then decorative rest, then mining. During a crisis, an idle colonist pulls the needed resource from a warehouse or its own inventory and delivers it to the relevant building. During repair, the closest available colonist is assigned and will interrupt mining if necessary. Decorative rest visits ensure colonists are visibly seen using dormitories and hospitals even when nothing is wrong. Mining occurs only when colonists are idle, deposits are available and a warehouse has storage room. Colonists carry their own inventory, mine deposits, fill to a sixty percent delivery threshold, then walk to the nearest warehouse with space and deposit what they have gathered. If no warehouse has room and their inventory is full, they stop mining rather than disappearing with resources.

Solar events fire periodically, spiking radiation. The flare class displayed on screen comes from the real NASA DONKI archive for May 2024, including the X8.7 flare of May fourteenth, the largest flare of Solar Cycle twenty-five. Without an active radiation shield, the player takes damage. With one, radiation decays safely. The trade-off is explicit: power diverted to shields is power lost to hydroponics, mining or repair.

Navigation is split between exterior and interior. Outside, colonists use a raycast whisker system with a fan of nine probes, adaptive backup, side commitment and progress detection to avoid oscillation. Inside buildings, they use a cable waypoint network with A star pathfinding, with the character controller disabled during traversal so stairs and tight interiors work reliably without clipping.

Interiors are instantiated per building. Each placed building spawns its own interior prefab at a unique offset, inactive until someone enters, giving full isolation. Two power plants have completely separate interiors, storage and repair pads, and simulation cost stays proportional to what is actually being used.

Damage accumulates over time. A timer selects a building and marks it damaged, starting a two-minute countdown. Repair pads inside the interior glow to guide the player or a colonist to the right spot. If the countdown expires, the building is destroyed. This forces the player to balance expansion against maintenance rather than simply building outward indefinitely.

Player vitals run in real time: health, hunger, stamina and injury. Colony conditions interact through an escalating crisis model. When hunger hits zero for the first time, a food crisis triggers. After the player eats, the system switches permanently to colony-food-based crisis detection. Sleeping is blocked during a crisis, and colony stats clamp at a twenty percent floor during sleep so the player cannot wake into an immediate emergency.

Game time runs separately from real time. A full day passes in twenty-four real minutes, and sleeping compresses eight game hours into five real seconds, with colony drain, production and the game clock all scaling by the same multiplier while player stats stay in real time.

Benefits. The project makes real engineering trade-offs tangible through play rather than explanation. Children experience the panic of running out of food, the relief of a shield absorbing a solar flare, the constraint of finite power and the consequence of building too fast. The game is replayable, with random damage events, deposit respawn and dual theaters meaning no two sessions are identical. It has a low barrier to entry, requiring only a Windows executable with no account or download beyond the build. Labels use plain language rather than jargon, so a child reads SHIELD NEEDED rather than radiation dose threshold exceeded, while the underlying simulation remains real.

Intended impact. Space-themed STEM content usually oversimplifies the trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Celestial Colonies makes the trade-off the mechanic. The intended impact is that a young player walks away understanding one true constraint of deep space survival, not just having played a fun game. That distinction between a themed game and a teaching tool is the core of the NASA challenge, and it is the standard the project holds itself to. The same simulation architecture extends naturally to communication delay, crew health modeling via OSDR biological data and live solar weather integration, so the project is a foundation rather than a ceiling.

Tools, coding languages and software. The project was built in Unity 6 using the Universal Render Pipeline for rendering, physics and scene management. All gameplay, artificial intelligence, navigation, user interface and data systems were written in C sharp. Microsoft Visual Studio and Visual Studio Code were used for code editing and debugging. NASA DONKI data was accessed through the Community Coordinated Modeling Center API at ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov and embedded as a JSON text asset loaded at runtime through the Resources system and parsed with Unity's JsonUtility. Google Stitch was used for user interface and user experience design ideation that informed the tactical aerospace terminal aesthetic. Descript and ElevenLabs were used for video editing and voice generation in the submission materials. The build targets Windows x86 sixty-four and was developed on a standard laptop by a single developer. No external asset packs were purchased or licensed. All gameplay logic, artificial intelligence, navigation, road mesh generation, interior systems and user interface code were written from scratch.

How the project is creative. The cascade model wires life-support systems into a circular dependency graph rather than treating them as independent bars. Power feeds oxygen production, oxygen feeds population survival and population increases drain on everything. The cascade is the mechanic, not just the theme. Real NASA data is used as a game mechanic rather than as decoration. The May 2024 archive sits inside the game, and every radiation event pulls a real flare class from that dataset. The X8.7 flare on the radiation banner is the actual largest flare of Solar Cycle twenty-five, the one that produced auroras visible in Florida and India. Priority-driven agents decide for themselves rather than following scripted sequences, so when a building is damaged the closest idle colonist stops what it is doing and walks over, and when oxygen drops, mining is abandoned and crisis resolution takes over. The behavior is emergent from the priority hierarchy rather than scripted per scenario. Roads are not flat quads: each tile is a subdivided mesh whose vertices sample terrain height, and adjacent tiles share edge coordinates so the road surface bends continuously with the terrain with no steps, no clipping and no z-fighting. Every placed building spawns its own isolated interior prefab at a unique world offset, inactive until entered, giving per-instance isolation that most games in this genre fake. The user interface uses plain language for a young audience while the systems underneath remain real, achieving accessibility without condescension.

Factors the team considered. Audience and accessibility were treated as primary constraints. Every label, prompt and crisis message was chosen to be readable at the seven to twelve age level, with flexibility so siblings, parents and classrooms can play the same build. Real engineering trade-offs were enforced by design: no safe choice exists in the game because every action costs a resource. Building a radiation shield costs three power per second, which is power not going to hydroponics or mining. Mining means walking away from base defense. Crisis resolution means abandoning mining. Every system was designed to have a cost and was tested against the question of whether a child could feel that cost. Radiation shielding was implemented as a full mechanic with a shield building, power cost, radiation bar and health drain when unshielded, tied to real NASA DONKI data so the numbers are not fabricated. Communication delay is displayed per theater at one point three seconds for the Moon and fourteen minutes for Mars, currently informational rather than wired into gameplay, and this limitation is stated honestly as post-launch scope rather than overstated. Real NASA data was embedded at build time with attribution shown in game, and the post-launch plan includes live API integration and OSDR biological data for crew health modeling. Replayability was built in through random damage events, deposit respawn and dual theaters so failure is instructive rather than punitive. Scope was chosen deliberately: the team shipped a feature-complete simulation rather than a broader but shallower demonstration, and save and load functionality was deferred to post-launch in favor of polishing the core simulation and closing the rubric gaps. Educational alignment was checked against every mechanic by asking what a child learns by playing with it. Features that did not teach something were cut or deprioritized even if they were fun.

Every decision costs something. That is the mission.
